posts.content:
Snowflake's coco team benchmarked GLM-5.2 vs Opus-4.7 on 103 dbt tasks. 
The results challenge some common assumptions.

 Pass@3: 66% vs 67% — effectively tied.
 Pass@1: 47.6% vs 53.7% — Opus wins by 6 percentage points.

 GLM is noisier per-trial, but broad enough at k=3 to stay competitive.

 What the data actually shows:

 ✅ "GLM takes more turns" — Confirmed. 99 turns avg vs 80 for Opus. 40 vs 29 execution-style calls per trial.

 ✅ "GLM uses 2× more tokens" — Confirmed. 860M vs 439M billing tokens. More turns, atomic API calls, and lower prompt-cache reuse (53% vs 96%).

 ✅ "GLM verifies more" — Partially confirmed. But it's atomized differently. GLM fires one sql_execute per check; Opus batches the same checks
 into fewer dbt show --inline calls. Same coverage, different shape.

 ❌ "GLM produces cleaner code" — Not supported. Pass@1 is 6pp lower. More verification ≠ more correct.

The real GLM edge: Dual-platform validation. The spec requires passing both DuckDB and Snowflake. GLM more consistently validates both targets — the causal factor behind several GLM-only wins.

 GLM's failure modes:

 1. Early folding. When it can't see the write path from reads alone, it exits without attempting. One task: 22 turns, 5 file reads, 0 writes, stop.
 2. Over-verification of wrong axes. One task: 411 tool calls, 24 minutes — checking row counts, distributions, nulls, column types, DuckDB/Snowflake parity. Failed. Opus solved it with 49 calls in 9 minutes.

Key insight: On tasks both models solve, GLM uses ~17% more calls — not 2×. The 2× framing is a whole-run average driven by tail tasks where GLM spirals.

Bottom line: Verification volume doesn't predict correctness. GLM's worst losses come from verifying the wrong axes exhaustively.

 #AI #Snowflake #LLM #MachineLearning #DataEngineering #dbt #Benchmarks

posts.content:
Two years ago, 31% of FinOps teams managed AI spend. Today it's 98%.

That is a massive shift. AI bills are hard. One agent can chain dozens of reasoning steps. One prompt can burn thousands of tokens. Costs move as fast as the outputs.

So we rebuilt cost management for the AI era. Two ways.

First, we put AI to work on the problem. Our coding agent CoCo now answers cost questions in plain English. "Why did compute spike Wednesday?" "Who is burning the most credits?"
  
No SQL. No digging through schemas. Spot an anomaly, click explain, get the story in seconds.

🚨 Exclusive: Snowflake CEO Says Better To Be Paranoid Than Confident About SaaSpocalypse

⚠️ While much of enterprise software is declaring the SaaSpocalypse over, Snowflake CEO Sridhar Ramaswamy is taking the opposite view. As AI agents continue lowering the cost and complexity of building software, he argues the biggest mistake companies can make is assuming yesterday’s advantages will survive tomorrow’s economics.

🎙️ I sat down with Ramaswamy at Snowflake Summit 2026 to discuss why AI coding costs, governance failures, and collapsing barriers to software creation are forcing enterprise leaders to rethink what durable value actually means.

💬 “I think it is better to be paranoid,” Ramaswamy told me, in an exclusive conversation. “Anyone who thinks this is a small change and they'll simply work their way through it—that's a bad mentality. Every company needs to internalize that creating software is just easier now.”

📊 The warning comes as the company continues to grow aggressively. It reported $1.39 billion in Q1 FY27 revenue, up 33% YoY, with 779 customers generating more than $1 million in trailing 12-month product revenue. It also committed $6 billion to Amazon Web Services (AWS) infrastructure and AI over five years.

🧩 Snowflake recently rebranded its two flagship products — CoWork, the always-on agent for knowledge workers, formerly Snowflake Intelligence, and CoCo, the coding agent for builders, formerly Cortex Code — and pushed both deeper into the tools enterprises already run, with extensions for Microsoft Excel, VS Code and Anthropic's Claude Code. Customers, including Synopsys Inc, WHOOP, Under Armour, Fanatics, and Thomson Reuters, are already utilizing the innovations.

📉 Ramaswamy also pushed back on the idea that SaaS disruption is already settled. In his view, the reshuffling of winners and losers has only just begun—and could take years to fully play out.
